The cushion starfish Asterina gibbosa begins its life cycle with the release of small, yolk-rich eggs into the surrounding seawater. The diameter of a mature egg prior to fertilisation is approximately 0.135 cm [Lb = approximately 0.135 cm], a measurement that places this species within the typical range for littoral asterinids. Following external fertilisation, the developing embryo undergoes a period of rapid cleavage and gastrulation while remaining within the protective egg envelope. The duration of embryonic development is temperature-dependent, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], larvae hatch successfully after roughly 20 days [ab = roughly 20 days]. This age at birth marks the transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to a free-swimming, planktotrophic bipinnaria larva. The newly hatched larva is minute, initially measuring less than a few hundred micrometres, and relies on ciliary feeding to capture phytoplankton from the water column. The 20-day incubation period at 12 °C is notably prolonged compared to some confamilial species from warmer waters, suggesting that local thermal regimes exert a strong influence on early developmental scheduling in this temperate echinoderm.

As the bipinnaria larva of Asterina gibbosa grows and develops within the plankton, it eventually reaches a stage of metamorphic competence and settles onto the benthos. The metamorphic transition involves a radical reorganisation of the larval body plan into the pentaradial form characteristic of juvenile starfish. This post-metamorphic juvenile then enters a period of sustained somatic growth. The species is relatively small-bodied, and the maximum total length ever recorded for a fully grown adult cushion starfish, measured from arm tip to opposite arm tip, is 5.0 cm [Li = 5.0 cm]. Individuals rarely exceed this size, making Asterina gibbosa one of the smaller members of its family in the north-eastern Atlantic. Growth rates in juveniles are influenced by food availability and water temperature, with most of the increase in body size occurring during the first few years of benthic life. The ultimate total length of 5.0 cm appears to represent a genuine asymptotic size, as older adults show negligible further increases in arm length, a pattern consistent with determinate or strongly decelerating growth in echinoderms.

Sexual maturation in Asterina gibbosa is a gradual process that begins when individuals reach a critical body size threshold. Field and laboratory studies indicate that the total length at which puberty is attained is approximately 1.5 cm [Lp = approximately 1.5 cm], measured from arm tip to arm tip across the oral surface. Below this size, the gonads remain undeveloped and gametogenesis has not yet commenced. The attainment of this 1.5 cm size threshold is a reliable morphological indicator of the onset of reproductive potential in this species. Juveniles below this size are exclusively in a pre-reproductive growth phase, allocating all available resources to somatic tissue rather than to gonadal production. The length at puberty of 1.5 cm represents roughly one-third of the ultimate total length of 5.0 cm, a ratio that is broadly consistent with life-history patterns observed in other small, iteroparous asteroids that reproduce annually. Populations in colder microhabitats may require a longer growth period to reach this critical size, but the morphological threshold itself appears to be a robust life-history invariant.

Under stable thermal conditions characteristic of their shallow subtidal and intertidal habitats, cushion starfish exhibit a well-defined schedule of reproductive and developmental milestones. In a laboratory population maintained at a year-round temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at which individuals first achieve sexual maturity is approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days], equivalent to roughly one year of benthic life following settlement and metamorphosis. This 365-day period to puberty is a critical life-history parameter, as it defines the age at which the population transitions from a juvenile to a potentially reproductive state. Some individuals from marginal habitats may require up to two years to reach full gonadal maturity, but the majority of cushion starfish in optimal conditions achieve this milestone within a single annual cycle. The age at puberty of one year at 12 °C suggests that this species is capable of an annual reproductive schedule, with juveniles settling in one summer potentially recruiting into the breeding population the following year. This relatively rapid maturation is typical of small-bodied, short-lived asteroids inhabiting seasonally productive environments.

Reproductive output in Asterina gibbosa has been quantified through long-term monitoring of captive individuals held under controlled environmental conditions. At a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females produce approximately 3 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3 eggs per spawning event], and with approximately 330 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 330 spawning events per year], the maximum annual reproductive output reaches about 1000 eggs per year [Ri = about 1000 eggs per year]. This combined expression of small clutch sizes and very high spawning frequency is an unusual reproductive strategy among temperate asteroids. In contrast to its prolific reproductive output, the maximum lifespan of Asterina gibbosa is surprisingly modest. Laboratory records maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] indicate that the oldest documented individuals survive for about 10 years [am = about 10 years], after which senescence and physiological deterioration become evident. This lifespan places Asterina gibbosa among the shorter-lived members of the Asterinidae, consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended somatic persistence.
